items.target: acute cholecystitis complicated by biliary peritonitis

claims.text: Case 1, an 80-year-old female, underwent total arch replacement for Stanford type A acute aortic dissection. Abdominal pain prompted evaluation alongside inflammatory markers. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 11.9 ×10³/μL and CRP 18.6 mg/dL. Gallstones were absent and the case was acalculous. Contrast CT showed reduced gallbladder-wall enhancement. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurred 9 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of same day, operative time 80 min and blood loss 15 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as diffuse on the dorsal side, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed necrosis from mucosa to outer fat-rich subserosal layer at leakage sites. No apparent RAS or perioperative cholecystectomy-related complications were reported. The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.

claims.text: Case 2, a 75-year-old female, had Stanford type A acute aortic dissection and cerebral infarction, and underwent total arch replacement for the dissection. Abdominal pain was explicitly absent; inflammatory-marker evaluation prompted imaging. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 17.1 ×10³/μL and CRP 12.9 mg/dL. Gallstones were absent and the case was acalculous. Contrast CT showed reduced gallbladder-wall enhancement. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurred 10 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of 5 days later, operative time 116 min and blood loss 12 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as neck, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed necrosis from mucosa to outer fat-rich subserosal layer at leakage sites. No apparent RAS or perioperative cholecystectomy-related complications were reported. The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.

items.target: acute cholecystitis complicated by biliary peritonitis

claims.text: Case 3, a 76-year-old male, underwent femoral-popliteal artery bypass for peripheral arterial disease. Abdominal pain prompted evaluation alongside inflammatory markers. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 12.4 ×10³/μL and CRP 29.9 mg/dL. Gallstones were absent and the case was acalculous. Noncontrast CT/MRI were used due to dialysis; Case 3 MRI suggested fundal bile leakage. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurred 3 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of 2 days later, operative time 140 min and blood loss 4 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as fundus, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed necrosis from mucosa to outer fat-rich subserosal layer at leakage sites. No apparent RAS or perioperative cholecystectomy-related complications were reported. The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.

items.target: acute cholecystitis complicated by biliary peritonitis

claims.text: Case 4, a 79-year-old male, underwent endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Abdominal pain was explicitly absent; inflammatory-marker evaluation prompted imaging. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 21.1 ×10³/μL and CRP 32.5 mg/dL. Gallstones were absent and the case was acalculous. Contrast CT showed reduced gallbladder-wall enhancement. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurred 5 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of same day, operative time 125 min and blood loss 10 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as diffuse, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed markedly thinned wall/full-thickness necrosis with layer structure difficult to evaluate. No apparent RAS or perioperative cholecystectomy-related complications were reported. The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.

claims.text: Case 5, an 80-year-old male, underwent ventricular septal defect closure (infarct exclusion method) for postmyocardial infarction ventricular septal rupture. Abdominal pain was explicitly absent; inflammatory-marker evaluation prompted imaging. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 10.5 ×10³/μL and CRP 17.7 mg/dL. Gallstones were present. Contrast CT showed reduced gallbladder-wall enhancement. Open cholecystectomy occurred 8 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of same day, operative time 72 min and blood loss 9 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as neck to body, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed multiple ulcers from mucosal to subserosal layer. RAS were identified, with leakage through them considered a possible mechanism. Severe heart failure/massive pleural effusion motivated open surgery; postoperative sputum retention required tracheostomy (grade IIIb). The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. The possibility of bile leakage from RAS was an author mechanism hypothesis rather than a confirmed separate diagnosis. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.
